summary: Discusses how privacy threats apply to IPv6 over various link layers and gives protocol designers advice on addressing them in adaptation-layer specifications. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Small devices can leak who and where they are through their addresses. This is advice on keeping those secrets.

questions: how many bits of entropy does an ipv6 interface identifier need
why are short addresses bad for ipv6 privacy
subtitle: How short or guessable IPv6 interface identifiers leak privacy, and what link-layer specs should do about it.

tldr.problem: IPv6 over low-power or constrained links often builds interface identifiers from short or fixed link-layer addresses, which have too little entropy and allow tracking and address scanning.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC works out how many bits of entropy are needed for a given link lifetime, reviews IEEE-identifier and Short Address approaches, and gives recommendations to authors of adaptation-layer specifications.
tldr.outcome: Specifications should explain how address scans are mitigated, include enough entropy for the maximum link lifetime, avoid padding Short Addresses with constant bits, and let addresses change over time and per network.

today: RFC 8065 is an Informational document and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is guidance for authors of adaptation-layer specifications for IPv6 over various link layers.

sections.title: The Privacy Problem
sections.content:
When interface identifiers (IIDs) are generated without enough entropy compared to the link lifetime, devices and users become vulnerable to threats discussed in RFC 6973 and RFC 7721. These include correlation of activities over time, location tracking when the same IID is used with different prefixes, device-specific vulnerability exploitation, and address scanning.

For links that may last for years, "enough" means at least 46 or so bits of entropy in a routable address, and ideally all 64 bits of the IID. Link-local addresses can also be exposed, since upper-layer protocols such as SMTP, SIP or DNS often leak them.

RFC 8064 recommends the address generation scheme of RFC 7217 rather than fixed link-layer addresses, and RFC 4941 defines temporary addresses for outbound sessions.
sections.eli5: If a device always uses the same easy-to-guess address, people can follow it from place to place and poke at it.

sections.title: How Much Entropy Is Needed
sections.content:
The threat that needs the most entropy is scanning of routable addresses. Many privacy-sensitive devices run in a stealth mode or sit behind a firewall that drops unsolicited traffic, so the scanner can only infer a host exists from the absence of an ICMP unreachable error. Routers typically rate limit those errors to 2 per second, which makes it take about a year to scan 26 bits of space.

The RFC derives a rule of thumb: bits of entropy needed = log2(devices per link) + log2(seconds of link lifetime) + 2. For up to 2^16 devices and an average link lifetime of 8 years (2^28 seconds), that gives at least 46 bits (16+28+2).

If addresses also provide security against spoofing, as CGAs and HBAs do, 59 or more bits are needed, because attackers are limited by processing power rather than ICMP rate limiting. If devices respond to unsolicited packets, more bits are needed still.
sections.eli5: The longer a secret code must stay safe and the more kids share the playground, the more digits it needs so nobody can guess it.

sections.title: Two Approaches to Link-Layer Addresses
sections.content:
Technologies usually offer IEEE identifiers, Short Addresses, or both. IEEE-identifier-based addresses (EUI-48 or EUI-64) make stateless LOWPAN_IPHC compression easy, but have too little entropy unless the identifier itself has enough and enough bits are carried into the IPv6 address. Per-network randomized link-layer addresses can mitigate threats other than correlation over time, and changing the link-layer address often enough, for example each time the link is established, can address that too.

Short Addresses padded with well-known constant bits lack the entropy to resist scanning unless the link is extremely short-lived, and an adversary could use statistics to infer the size of the address space and so the technology in use. When Short Addresses are wanted, the IID could be built with a one-way hash of a shared secret (such as the key needed to join the layer-2 network) and the Short Address. That spreads IIDs over the full 64-bit space while keeping full stateless compression.
sections.eli5: Short numbers are easy to guess. Mixing a short number with a secret the group shares makes a long, scrambled one that is still quick to use.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
For adaptation-layer specifications the RFC recommends:

  • Say in the privacy or security section how address scans are mitigated, by short-lived links, many bits of entropy, or both, and show the entropy is enough for the maximum link lifetime.
  • Define a way to include sufficient bits of entropy in the IID, for example by allowing randomized link-layer addresses.
  • Do not simply pad a Short Address with constant bits, unless the link lifetime is guaranteed to be extremely short or the network allocates the Short Address.
  • Make sure an IPv6 address can change over long periods, to mitigate correlation over time.
  • If a device can roam and the IID has more than a few bits of entropy, let the IID vary per network, to mitigate location tracking.
sections.eli5: Make addresses long enough to be hard to guess, and let them change when you move or after a while.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says only that the whole document is about security considerations and how to specify possible mitigations. It adds no protocol of its own and no IANA actions are described in the text. Its guidance applies to the specifications that define IPv6 over particular link layers.
sections.eli5: The whole document is about keeping things safe, so there is no extra safety section to add.
